flashcards.q: Why does fixed-epsilon epsilon-greedy have LINEAR regret?
flashcards.a: A constant fraction epsilon of every round (forever, not just early on) is spent choosing uniformly at random, including arms already confidently known to be bad -- this constant per-round expected regret contribution sums to linear growth in total rounds, unlike UCB/Thompson's logarithmic regret.

flashcards.q: UCB1 formula and the statistical principle behind it?
flashcards.a: argmax(mean_i + sqrt(2*ln(t)/n_i)). The bonus comes from a Chernoff-Hoeffding bound: with high probability mean_i+bonus_i upper-bounds the true mean. 'Optimism under uncertainty' -- act as if every arm is as good as its plausible best case; bonus shrinks as n_i grows, auto-tapering exploration -> O(log t) regret.

flashcards.q: Thompson sampling for Bernoulli arms -- update rule and selection rule?
flashcards.a: Beta(1,1) prior, update to Beta(alpha+1,beta) on success / Beta(alpha,beta+1) on failure (closed-form conjugate). Sample ONE value per arm's posterior each round, pick the arm with the highest SAMPLE (not highest mean) -- wide (uncertain) posteriors naturally get explored more.

flashcards.q: LinUCB: how does it extend UCB to context, and what's the confidence bonus derived from?
flashcards.a: Per-arm ridge regression theta_i_hat=(D_i^T D_i+lambda*I)^-1 D_i^T c_i estimates reward as x.theta_i. Bonus = alpha*sqrt(x^T(D_i^TD_i+lambda*I)^-1 x), from the ridge regression's own uncertainty -- grows in under-explored directions of context space, personalizing explore/exploit per context.

flashcards.q: Why doesn't a raw high-cardinality user ID help LinUCB generalize across users?
flashcards.a: LinUCB's benefit comes from sharing statistical strength across similar contexts via the linear model. A raw ID with no inherent structure gives nothing to generalize from -- it must see that exact ID before learning anything about it, same as one-hot IDs offering no cross-category information transfer elsewhere in this track.

flashcards.q: Define cumulative regret and why it's the correct bandit evaluation metric.
flashcards.a: sum_t(best_arm_reward - chosen_arm_reward). Correct because it penalizes the COST of exploration itself, not just whether the algorithm eventually found the best arm -- an algorithm that converges correctly but wastes huge reward getting there has high regret despite 'succeeding'.

flashcards.q: Why must an exploring bandit sometimes serve a suboptimal option to a real user, and what's the production safeguard?
flashcards.a: By definition, any exploring algorithm must occasionally choose a non-best-known arm to gather information, or it's pure exploitation with no correction mechanism. Safeguard: an explicit safety floor excluding catastrophic options from the exploration set, or a hard cap on exploration traffic share.

flashcards.q: Why can't you evaluate a new bandit policy by naively averaging old-policy logged rewards for actions the new policy would pick?
flashcards.a: Old-policy logs contain outcomes at a frequency proportional to how often the OLD policy chose each action -- restricting to 'rounds where policies agree' conditions on a biased subsample, not an unbiased estimate of the new policy's full-deployment performance. Fix: inverse propensity scoring, reweighting by 1/P(old policy chose this action).

flashcards.q: Bandit vs fixed-horizon A/B test -- when is each the right tool?
flashcards.a: Bandit: ongoing/repeated decisions where allocation should adapt continuously (recommendation ranking, pricing). Fixed A/B test: one-time permanent ship/no-ship decision between a small set of variants, where rigorous significance testing matters more than continuous adaptation.
